title: Threads Between Names
setting: a conspiracy wall of red string

post.author: u/red_string_merriam
post.title: I'm a local historian with a red-string wall in my spare room. I let a model build a second wall from the town's records. It tied two events sixty years apart to one man, who died in 1921.

blocks.text: I live in Ashlock, a small town on the edge of the fens. For eleven years the back wall of my spare room has been cork board: photocopies, index cards, and red string between anything that touches anything else. Visitors call it my conspiracy wall. I call it the town.

This spring the history society had the town's records scanned: council minutes, planning files and clippings from the Ashlock Courier, 4,960 records, cut into 7,480 chunks. My nephew set up a tool called GraphRAG. A model reads each chunk and pulls out every name, which the tool calls an entity, and every link between two names, a relationship, each with the record it came from. Then it groups closely linked names into communities and writes a summary of each. One model call per chunk just to read them; it ran all night. A wall that builds itself.
On Thursday I asked it the question for my talk.

21:12  ask    What connects the 1894 fence petition to the 1954 chapel fire?
21:12  graph  E. Tallentire. In 1894 he moved to decline the petition to
              fence Long Pond. In 1954 he raised the alarm at the chapel fire.

I had never seen those two together. I found the 1894 minutes and the 1954 clipping in my boxes and pinned a red string between them. Then I looked him up. The Courier ran his obituary in January 1921: Mr Ezekiel Tallentire, tanner, of Tanpit Lane, aged 60.
The man who raised the alarm in 1954 had been dead for thirty-three years.

The tool can show the path behind an answer: each step, which it calls a hop, is one relationship from one record. I copied the ten records around the thread, numbered them R1 to R10, and drew what it showed me.

blocks.label: the_thread.png

diagram.aria: Merriam's drawing of the tool's path. Left: the fence petition of 1894, from R1, where E. Tallentire moved to decline it. Middle: one E. Tallentire node, built from 4 records. Right: the chapel fire of 15 March 1954, from R8, where E. Tallentire raised the alarm. Below the middle node: R6, January 1921, his death, aged 60. The path is 2 hops.

blocks.caption: Drawn from the tool's path on Friday morning. Hop 1, from R1, the council minutes of 3 September 1894: petition to fence Long Pond declined, moved by Cllr E. Tallentire, tanner, of Tanpit Lane. Hop 2, from R8, the Courier of 16 March 1954: alarm raised at 02:10 by Mr E. Tallentire, of Tenter Row. The tool says the node was built from 4 records: R1, his obituary of January 1921 (R6), a planning file of 1953 (R7) and R8.

blocks.text: I once read on here about a house museum whose séance mixed up two women who shared a name. I thought that was a search problem. Mine has string. Tenter Row is across town from Tanpit Lane. The talk is in three weeks. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nobody is walking out of 1921 to report a fire. What your nephew built has names. The entities and relationships together are a knowledge graph: a network of things and the links between them. GraphRAG is Microsoft's method of building one with a model and answering from it. Your question is a multi-hop question: its answer needs several records joined, because no single record names both ends. Asking for the main threads in all 4,960 records would be a whole-collection question, which no handful of chunks can answer. Two questions. What does each of the four records behind that node say about where he lived and how old he was? And when your nephew's old chunk search got the same question, what did it send, and what did it say?

replies.author: u/red_string_merriam
replies.text: R1, 1894: Cllr E. Tallentire, tanner, of Tanpit Lane. R6, January 1921: Mr Ezekiel Tallentire, tanner, of Tanpit Lane, died aged 60. R7, May 1953: Ezekiel Tallentire, aged 22, of Tenter Row, applies to open a cycle repair shop. R8, March 1954: Mr E. Tallentire, of Tenter Row. The old chunk search sent its top 3, R8, R1 and R2, and joined R1 to R8 on the name. Same answer, no string.

comments.author: u/one_graph_swithin
comments.text: Graphs are the future of RAG. Put everything in one. Chunks are a pile of paper; a graph knows how the town fits together. Send every question through it, facts included, and you have one index, one way of asking, and nothing left to keep in step. Your graph found something your boxes never showed you in eleven years. Don't go backwards now.

replies.author: u/red_string_merriam
replies.text: Even for asking what night the chapel burned?

replies.author: u/one_graph_swithin
replies.text: Especially that. Every fact is a connection if you look.

comments.author: u/tenter_row_crispin
comments.text: The Ezekiel Tallentire on Tenter Row was my grandad. He was in his twenties, he saw the smoke from his bedroom window and ran for the phone box. He'd opened the cycle shop the year before. He never sat on any council and he never met the tanner; he only found out there'd been another Ezekiel Tallentire when somebody showed him the old tannery's sign. He'd not have liked being tied to a vote against a fence round a pond.

replies.author: u/red_string_merriam
replies.text: I'm sorry. The string is coming down. I'll bring you a copy of the clipping.

reply.prompt: The talk is in three weeks, and the society wants the tool kept for its next project. What should Merriam change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send every question through the graph, the facts as well, so all answers come from one index that knows the links.
options.part2: We sent every question through the graph. My nephew rebuilt the index first, another 7,480 extraction calls, one per chunk, and another night. Then the talk's questions. On what night did the chapel burn, and who raised the alarm? The graph answered from the Tallentire node: the alarm was raised by E. Tallentire, tanner and councillor, who died in 1921 aged 60. The old chunk search had got that one right from the 1954 clipping alone. The connection question still ran petition, E. Tallentire, fire: 2 hops, R1 and R8. Asked for the town's main threads, it read 3 community summaries, and one of them said a single man joins the pond and the fire. The string stayed up, and now it was in the fact answers too.
options.senior: A graph is a second index, not a better first one. For a fact that sits in one record, chunk retrieval finds the record and quotes it; the graph answers from entity descriptions that a model wrote, so any extraction error, here a merge of two men, travels into answers that were right before. Use the graph where it earns its indexing cost: connection and whole-collection questions.

options.text: Keep plain chunk search, and send the top 8 instead of the top 3 for connection questions, so the chain is all there.
options.verdict: The chain was there; the name won
options.part2: We kept the chunk search and sent the top 8 for connection questions. The eight were R8, R1, R2, R9, R10, R4, R3 and R5, and the true chain was in front of the model: the 1897 filling of Long Pond, the chapel on plot 4, the inquiry's cracked gas pipe. It still joined R1 to R8 on the name E. Tallentire, one join instead of two, and gave the same answer. Every question now sent eight records instead of three. Asked for the town's main threads, the top 8 found 3 of 4 and said nothing about Tenter Row.
options.senior: More chunks put more records in front of the model, but nothing in them says which E. Tallentire is which, and the shortest join is still the shared name. Multi-hop questions need the hops made explicit, with each entity checked before two mentions become one, and whole-collection questions need every part of the collection summarized, not a bigger top-k.

options.text: Chunks for facts, the graph for links and whole-town questions; check dates and places before merging; show the path.
options.part2: We kept the chunk search for facts and the graph for connection and whole-town questions, rebuilt after one change: two people with the same name became one only if the place matched and the dates fit one life. That cost another 7,480 extraction calls overnight. The four records split into two men: Ezekiel Tallentire, 1861 to 1921, of Tanpit Lane, and Ezekiel Tallentire, born 1931, of Tenter Row. On the ten records the graph went from 14 entities to 15 and from 3 communities to 4, and indexing them took 27 model calls instead of 25. The connection question now returns 4 hops, each shown with its record: the petition to Long Pond (R1), Long Pond to plot 4 (R4), plot 4 to the gas pipe (R9), the gas pipe to the fire (R9). The chapel was built on the filled-in pond, and the old ground settled and cracked the pipe. The night of the fire came from the chunk search: 15 March 1954, 02:10, Mr E. Tallentire of Tenter Row (R8), one model call. The main threads: 4 of 4, from 5 calls. The red string came down, and a new one went up, from the pond to the chapel floor.
options.senior: Use each index for what it is good at. Chunk retrieval answers facts that sit in one record, cheaply. The graph answers questions that need several records joined, by following a path, and questions about the whole collection, by reading community summaries. Its weak point is extraction: a wrong merge draws a thread between strangers, so resolve entities with whatever metadata you have, dates, places, identifiers, before merging, and show every hop with its source so a reader can check the thread.

options.text: Switch the tool off and go on building the wall by hand, reading every record and checking every name myself, as before.
options.part2: I switched the tool off and went back to the wall. The ten records around the thread took me an hour, 6 minutes each, and I got all three questions right: two Tallentires, the pond under the chapel, the four threads. Then I did the sums for the rest: 4,960 records at 6 minutes each is 496 hours, and the Courier's archive keeps adding clippings. The talk went ahead with one pond and one chapel, and the other 4,950 records stayed in their boxes.
options.senior: Reading by hand is the most careful extraction there is, and it doesn't scale: the cost grows with every record and starts again with every new box. Keep the person where judgement matters, deciding the merges the rules can't settle and checking the paths the answers show, and let the graph do the reading.

sim.title: Trace the Ashlock threads yourself
sim.lede: You're Merriam on Friday morning, with the ten records around the thread, R1 to R10, and the knowledge graph the tool pulled from them: 22 relationships, each with its source record, and 14 entities on the night, 15 once the two E. Tallentires are kept apart. There is no real model and no live extraction; the graph is stated. Same-name people: merge by name, as the tool did, joins every mention with the same first initial and surname into one node; check dates and places joins a mention to a person only if the place matches and the year falls inside that person's known life. Three questions: a fact (the night of the fire and who raised the alarm), a connection (what links the 1894 petition to the 1954 fire) and a whole-collection question (the main threads). Chunks: each record is one chunk with a stated stand-in similarity to each question, and the top 3 or top 8 are sent; a stand-in answerer joins two sent records only when they name the same thing, people by first initial and surname, taking the fewest joins. In chunk mode a hop is one join between two records; in graph mode, one relationship. The graph: a connection is the shortest path from the fire to the petition, relationships read in the order listed; a fact comes from the fire's relationships and the node at the other end; a whole-collection question reads every community summary, one model call each, plus one to combine them. Indexing: one extraction call per chunk, one summary call for each entity, or pair of entities, described by more than one record, and one call per community summary. By hand: 6 minutes a record. The full collection is 4,960 records in 7,480 chunks.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the night: merged by name, the connection question, the graph. The false thread: petition to E. Tallentire (R1) to the fire (R8), 2 hops, one Tallentire node built from 4 records, 25 indexing calls. Switch to check dates and places: two Tallentires, and the path becomes 4 hops through Long Pond, plot 4 and the gas pipe (R1, R4, R9), 27 indexing calls. Answer from chunks: top 3 or top 8, R1 is joined to R8 on the name, 1 hop. Ask the fact question: chunks are right from R8 with no indexing calls; on the merged graph the man who raised the alarm died in 1921. Ask the whole-collection question: chunks find 2 of 4 threads (top 3) or 3 of 4 (top 8); the checked graph finds 4 of 4 from 5 calls, the merged one 3, one of them false. Answer by hand: right every time, and 496 h for the full collection. Read the community summaries with each merge setting.

explain.oneLine: Nothing walked out of 1921. The model pulled the name E. Tallentire out of an 1894 minute and a 1954 clipping, the indexer merged every mention of that name into one node, and the shortest path between the petition and the fire ran through a man made of two.

steps.title: Two men, one node.
steps.text: Indexing reads each chunk and writes down entities and relationships, then merges what looks the same. Microsoft's GraphRAG documentation says it plainly: any entities with the same title and type are merged by creating an array of their descriptions. Merriam's E. Tallentire of 1894 and E. Tallentire of 1954 had the same name and the same type, a person, so they became one node built from 4 records: a tanner who moved to decline a petition, died in 1921 aged 60, applied for a cycle shop in 1953 and raised an alarm in 1954. The shortest path from the petition to the fire went through him: 2 hops, R1 and R8.

steps.title: Why chunk search couldn't answer it either.
steps.text: The true connection needs three records, none of which names both ends: R1 (the petition was about Long Pond), R4 (the chapel stood on plot 4, the old pond) and R9 (the old ground settled and cracked the gas pipe under the chapel). That is a multi-hop question. Chunk search sends the passages most like the question, here R8, R1 and R2, and the answer joined the two that share a name. Sending the top 8 put the whole chain in front of the model, but the name was still the shortest join. Whole-collection questions fail in a different way: 3 chunks cover 3 records, and asked for the main threads, the top 3 found 2 of 4.

steps.title: What the graph adds: paths and community summaries.
steps.text: GraphRAG builds the knowledge graph with a model, groups closely linked entities into communities with a clustering method called Leiden, and has the model summarize each community. Edge and colleagues, who introduced it, describe a graph index built in two stages: first an entity knowledge graph, then community summaries for all groups of closely related entities. A connection question follows a path between two entities. A whole-collection question uses every community summary to write a partial answer and combines them, which in the sim reads 4 summaries in 4 calls plus 1 to combine, and finds 4 of 4 threads.

steps.title: Check before you merge: entity resolution.
steps.text: Entity resolution is deciding whether two mentions are the same real thing. A name is weak evidence; dates and places are stronger. The sim's rule: a mention joins a person only if the place matches and the year falls inside that person's known life. R1 and R6 (Tanpit Lane, 1894 and 1921) are one man, 1861 to 1921; R7 and R8 (Tenter Row, 1953 and 1954) are another, born 1931. The graph grows from 14 entities to 15, from 3 communities to 4, and the path becomes petition, Long Pond, plot 4, gas pipe, fire: 4 hops, R1, R4 and R9. Where the evidence is thin, keep the mentions apart and ask a person.

steps.title: Show the path, and keep chunks for facts.
steps.text: An answer about a connection should show every hop with its record, so the reader can check each link; Merriam found the false thread only because the tool showed R1 and R8. Facts that sit in one record, like the night of the fire, come back right from chunk search with one model call and no graph at all. The graph costs at indexing: one extraction call per chunk, 7,480 for Ashlock, plus summaries and community reports, and a rebuild when the records change. When a graph grows large, it can live in a graph database such as Neo4j, which stores relationships beside their nodes so that following a path is a cheap traversal (Dead Letter's curiosity shop case).

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row, the path the checked graph returns, left to right: the fence petition, Long Pond, plot 4, the gas pipe, the chapel fire, with the hops labelled R1, R4, R9 and R9. Bottom row: Ezekiel Tallentire, 1861 to 1921, of Tanpit Lane, linked to the petition by R1; Ezekiel Tallentire, born 1931, of Tenter Row, linked to the fire by R8; between them, the merge check: same name, different place and dates, two people.

notes.text: the path, 4 hops, each with its record

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the talk. The merge check keeps two Ezekiel Tallentires apart, because the places and dates don't fit one life. The connection question now follows the ground instead of a name: petition to Long Pond (R1), Long Pond to plot 4 (R4), plot 4 to the gas pipe (R9), the gas pipe to the fire (R9). Facts such as the night of the fire still come from chunk search.

fix.title: The fix: two indexes, a merge check, and the path on every answer
fix.text: Keep chunk search for facts: the night of the fire comes back from R8 with one model call. Use the graph for connection and whole-collection questions, but rebuild it with a merge check: two mentions with the same name become one entity only if the place matches and the dates fit one life, and unclear cases stay apart for Merriam to decide. On the ten records that splits E. Tallentire into two men, gives 15 entities and 4 communities, and costs 27 indexing calls instead of 25; on the full collection it means another 7,480 extraction calls. Then show every connection answer as its path, each hop with its record: petition, Long Pond (R1), plot 4 (R4), gas pipe (R9), fire (R9).

limits: A merge check is only as good as the metadata. Many records carry no address or age, and the same rule that kept the Tallentires apart can split one person recorded under two names. Somebody still has to decide the unclear cases.

The graph is expensive to build and to keep: one extraction call per chunk, 7,480 for Ashlock, plus summaries and community reports, and a rebuild or an incremental update whenever records are added or corrected. Microsoft's own guide warns that it can consume a lot of LLM resources.
A path shows how the graph linked two things, not that the link is true. Each hop is a model's reading of one record, so the reader still has to open the records and check them.

explain.seniorTake: Chunk retrieval answers questions whose answer sits in one place. It struggles when the answer has to be assembled from several records or from the whole collection. A knowledge graph helps with exactly those two, and it buys that help with model calls at indexing time and with a new kind of error: the graph is a model's reading of your data, so a wrong merge or a missed relationship becomes a confident thread. Treat entity resolution as part of the design, not a clean-up job, using whatever identifiers, dates and places the data carries, and make every graph answer show its path with sources. Keep plain retrieval for facts, and decide per question type which index answers.

realWorld.title: Edge and colleagues, 2024: RAG fails on global questions
realWorld.text: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization (arXiv 2404.16130, first submitted 24 April 2024) says RAG fails on global questions directed at an entire text corpus, such as "What are the main themes in the dataset?", since this is inherently a query-focused summarization (QFS) task, rather than an explicit retrieval task.

realWorld.title: Edge and colleagues: a graph index in two stages
realWorld.text: The same abstract says the approach uses an LLM to build a graph index in two stages: first, to derive an entity knowledge graph from the source documents, then to pregenerate community summaries for all groups of closely related entities. Given a question, each community summary is used to generate a partial response, before all partial responses are again summarized in a final response. For global sensemaking questions over datasets in the 1 million token range, it reports substantial improvements over a conventional RAG baseline for both the comprehensiveness and diversity of generated answers.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: connecting the dots
realWorld.text: Microsoft's GraphRAG documentation says baseline RAG struggles to connect the dots, which happens when answering a question requires traversing disparate pieces of information through their shared attributes, and performs poorly when asked to holistically understand summarized semantic concepts over large data collections. Those are Merriam's two kinds of question: the connection and the main threads.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: the indexing steps
realWorld.text: The same page lists the steps: slice up an input corpus into a series of TextUnits, which provide fine-grained references in the outputs; extract all entities, relationships, and key claims from the TextUnits; perform a hierarchical clustering of the graph using the Leiden technique; and generate summaries of each community and its constituents from the bottom-up.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: four ways to ask
realWorld.text: It lists Global Search for reasoning about holistic questions about the corpus by leveraging the community summaries, Local Search for reasoning about specific entities by fanning-out to their neighbors, DRIFT Search, which adds community information to local search, and Basic Search for those times when your query is best answered by baseline RAG (standard top k vector search). Even the tool keeps plain retrieval for some questions.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: same title, one entity
realWorld.text: The dataflow page says each TextUnit's subgraph lists entities with a title, type, and description, and that these subgraphs are merged together: any entities with the same title and type are merged by creating an array of their descriptions, which a model then summarizes into a single description. That is the step that made two Ezekiel Tallentires one.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: global search is map and reduce
realWorld.text: The global search page says it uses community reports as context data to generate a response in a map-reduce manner: each chunk of reports produces an intermediate response of rated points, and the most important points are aggregated into the final response. Lower hierarchy levels tend to yield more thorough responses but may also increase the time and LLM resources needed.

realWorld.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: the cost warning
realWorld.text: The getting-started guide warns that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources, and recommends starting with the tutorial dataset and experimenting with fast, inexpensive models before committing to a big indexing job.

asked: When would you use GraphRAG instead of plain RAG?
What does entity resolution mean, and why does it matter?
How do you answer questions about a whole document collection?
interview.answer: Plain RAG retrieves the few chunks most like the question, which works when the answer sits in one place. It struggles with two kinds of question: multi-hop ones, where the answer needs several documents joined and none names both ends, and whole-collection ones, like what are the main themes, where k chunks only ever cover k chunks. GraphRAG has a model extract entities and relationships from every chunk into a knowledge graph, clusters the graph into communities and summarizes each. Connection questions follow a path through the graph; whole-collection questions map over the community summaries and combine the partial answers. The costs: at least one model call per chunk at indexing, plus summaries and reports, and rebuilds as the data changes; and extraction errors become false links. The worst is a bad merge, two people with the same name made one, which is why entity resolution matters: deciding whether two mentions are the same thing using metadata such as IDs, dates and places, keeping uncertain cases apart. I'd keep plain retrieval for facts, use the graph for connection and global questions, and show every graph answer's path with its sources.

terms.def: Someone who researches the history of one town or district, usually from its records, newspapers and people.
A board covered with documents and photos joined by string, as in crime films. Merriam's is real and holds eleven years of research.
On Merriam's wall, a string pinned between two documents that are connected. In the story, a thread is any claimed link between two things.
Low, flat, wet land in eastern England, much of it drained for farming.
A local club of people interested in their area's past, which often collects and preserves records.
The written record of what a town council discussed and decided at each meeting.
The council's file on an application to build, change or use a property, with its decision.
An article cut, or copied, from a newspaper.
The town's local newspaper in the story.
A tanner turns animal hides into leather; a tannery is the works where it is done.
A written request signed by many people and sent to someone in authority. Here, the Pond Cottages families asked the council to fence Long Pond.
Short for councillor, an elected member of a town council.
Formally proposed something for a council to vote on. E. Tallentire moved that the petition be declined.
Waste material dug out or thrown away, here from the tannery, used to fill Long Pond.
A Methodist place of worship. Ashlock's was built on plot 4 of Kiln Street and opened in 1902.
A numbered piece of land laid out for building. Plot 4 of Kiln Street stands on the filled-in pond.
An official investigation into what happened. The council's 1954 inquiry found the old pond ground had settled and cracked a gas pipe.
A newspaper notice of someone's death, usually with a short account of their life.
A thing a model pulls out of text as a node in a knowledge graph: a person, place, organization, event or object.
A link between two entities pulled out of a record, such as raised the alarm at, kept with the record it came from.
A network of entities and the relationships between them, built so a program can follow links from one thing to another.
Microsoft's method: a model extracts a knowledge graph from the chunks, groups it into communities, summarizes each, and answers from the graph and the summaries.
One model call that reads a chunk and writes down the entities and relationships in it. GraphRAG makes at least one per chunk.
A group of entities more closely linked to each other than to the rest of the graph, found by a clustering method.
A short report a model writes about one community and its members at indexing time. GraphRAG's documents also call it a community report.
A chain of relationships from one entity to another. A shortest path uses the fewest relationships.
One step along a path: one relationship in the graph, or, in the sim's chunk mode, one join between two records.
A question whose answer needs several records joined, because no single record holds both ends.
A question about the entire collection, such as its main themes, that no small set of chunks can answer. Edge and colleagues call these global questions.
In the sim, treating every mention with the same first initial and surname as one person. Close to GraphRAG's default of merging entities with the same title and type.
One place in one record where a name appears. Four mentions of E. Tallentire made one node on the night.
One entity in a graph, drawn as a box. Here, the merged E. Tallentire was one node built from 4 records.
Deciding whether two mentions refer to the same real thing before merging them, using evidence such as identifiers, dates and places.
The sim's entity resolution rule: a mention joins a person only if the place matches and the year falls inside that person's known life.
The sim's rule in place of a model for chunk mode: it joins two sent records only when they name the same thing, taking the fewest joins.
A score the sim states for each record and question in place of a real embedding comparison.
The ten records around the thread that Merriam copied and numbered, out of the town's 4,960.
The work done once, ahead of questions, to make records searchable: here, embedding chunks or extracting and summarizing a graph.
Run indexing again over the collection, needed after changing how it is built, such as the merge rule.
GraphRAG's name for a chunk: the piece of text it extracts from, kept so answers can point back to it.
A method for finding communities in a graph. GraphRAG uses a hierarchical version, which splits large communities into smaller ones.
Grouping things into clusters, then clusters within clusters, giving levels from broad to detailed.
GraphRAG's query mode for questions about specific entities: it starts from the entity and fans out to its neighbours.
GraphRAG's query mode for questions about the whole collection: it answers from every community summary and combines the answers.
A GraphRAG query mode that starts from specific entities like local search but adds community information.
GraphRAG's query mode that does plain top-k vector search over chunks, for questions best answered that way.
Splitting work into many independent parts (map), then combining their results into one (reduce).
Writing a summary of a body of text that answers a particular question.
In Edge and colleagues' paper, a question that asks for an understanding of a whole dataset rather than one fact.
The paper's two measures of an answer: how much of the question it covers, and how many different perspectives it gives.
Large language model.
Microsoft's name for ordinary RAG: retrieve chunks by vector similarity and send them to the model.
A free public website where researchers post papers, often before formal publication.
Updating an index with only the records that were added or changed, instead of rebuilding it all.
Customer relationship management: the system a company keeps its customer records and contact history in.
A card payment reversed by the customer's bank after the customer disputes it.
Another name the same person or company is known by, such as a maiden name or a trading name.
The surname a woman had before marriage, when she takes her husband's surname.
Checking a company or person carefully before a deal, such as an investment or a purchase.
A person appointed to manage a company and named in its official registry filings.
The unique number a national company registry gives each company; some registries also give directors identifiers.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012, which sets rules for how organizations collect, use and disclose personal data.
Section 23 of the PDPA: a reasonable effort to make personal data accurate and complete if it is likely to be used to decide about the person or disclosed.
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark, a certification that an organization's data protection practices meet the PDPA and related standards.

atWork: Look for any place where your systems join records about people or companies by name: a CRM merge, a supplier list, a knowledge graph over contracts or tickets. A common incident: a due-diligence team builds a graph over company filings and news, and it links two companies through a shared director. The director turns out to be two different people with the same name, in different countries, one of them with a bad record; the graph had merged them, and the risk flag landed on the wrong deal. The fix was entity resolution on identifiers: companies matched by their registry registration numbers, directors by registry identifiers and dates of appointment, and any name-only match held apart for an analyst. Check what your own merges use. If it is the name, find an identifier, a date or a place to add, keep unsure matches apart, and make every link the system shows carry the record it came from. Standards-readiness note: if your organization processes personal data under Singapore's PDPA, or holds or is pursuing the Data Protection Trustmark (DPTM), section 23 (the Accuracy Obligation) asks for a reasonable effort to ensure personal data is accurate and complete where it is likely to be used to make a decision that affects the individual or to be disclosed to another organization; two people merged into one record is exactly such an inaccuracy, so build the merge check and its evidence into the first design rather than finding it at assessment time.

recall.prompt: Your support team's assistant answers from a knowledge graph built from five years of tickets. An agent asks why a customer's refund was refused, and the answer says the customer had a chargeback dispute in 2021. The agent finds two customer records with the same full name: one in Leeds who disputed a charge in 2021, one in Bristol who signed up in 2024. What went wrong, what do you change, and what should every connection answer show?

keyIdeas.idea: The graph merged two different customers who share a name into one node, so the 2021 dispute became a false link to the 2024 customer
Resolve entities with metadata before merging: customer ID first, then city and dates, keeping unsure matches apart
Show the path with the source record of every hop, so the agent can check the link

recall.model: The graph merged two different customers who share a name into one node when it was built, so the shortest path from the refusal ran through a person made of two: the Leeds customer's 2021 dispute became a false link to the Bristol customer. I'd add entity resolution before merging: two mentions become one customer only if the metadata agrees, the customer ID first, then the city and the dates, and anything unsure stays apart and goes to a person. Then rebuild the graph, and make every connection answer show the path with the source record of each hop, so the agent can see the dispute came from a different account.

recall.prompt: Which kind of question does plain chunk retrieval, the top k passages by similarity, usually handle worst?
options: A fact stated in one passage, such as the date of an event
A question that needs several documents joined, or a summary of the whole collection
A question that repeats words from the passage that answers it
A question about a document added yesterday
recall.why: Top-k retrieval returns the few passages most like the question. A fact in one passage is its best case. A multi-hop question needs passages that may not resemble the question at all, the middle of the chain, and a whole-collection question needs every part of the data, while k chunks cover only k chunks. Those two are where a knowledge graph and community summaries help.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: when would you use GraphRAG instead of retrieving chunks, and what does it cost? Answer as you would in the room.

keyIdeas.idea: Connection (multi-hop) questions and whole-collection questions, where no single chunk holds the answer
Indexing costs model calls per chunk plus summaries and community reports, and has to be redone as data changes
Keep chunk retrieval for facts, and guard against extraction errors such as wrongly merged names; show the path

recall.model: I'd reach for GraphRAG when the questions are about connections or about the whole collection. A multi-hop question, how is A linked to C, needs several documents joined, and top-k retrieval usually brings back the ends but not the middle; a whole-collection question, what are the main themes, needs every part of the data, and k chunks cover k chunks. GraphRAG extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph, groups them into communities and summarizes each, so connection questions follow a path and global questions read the community summaries. The cost is at indexing: at least one model call per chunk, plus summaries and community reports, and a rebuild when the data changes. And extraction errors become false links: a wrong merge of two people with the same name draws a thread between strangers, so I'd do entity resolution with dates, places or IDs, show the path with its sources, and keep plain chunk retrieval for fact questions, where it is cheaper and just as good.

recall.prompt: How does GraphRAG's global search answer a question such as "what are the main themes in this collection?"
options: It retrieves the 5 chunks most similar to the question and sends them to the model
It finds the entity named in the question and follows its relationships
It uses each community summary to write a partial answer, then combines the partial answers into one
It sends the whole collection to the model in one call
recall.why: Global search works over the community summaries written at indexing time, in a map-reduce manner: each summary, or chunk of summaries, gives a partial answer, and the most important points are combined into the final response. Following an entity's relationships is local search, and the top 5 chunks is basic search.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The graph now checks dates and places before it merges anyone, and the talk went well: the pond under the chapel got a gasp. Now the society is writing a history of the town school, and the graph says the 1919 schoolmistress and the 1925 headmistress have no connection at all. A retired teacher on the committee says they were the same woman: she married in 1922, and the minutes switched to her married name. The graph has her as two people, and every question about the school's first woman head comes back half answered.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the graph see two women, and what should the merge check do about it?

keyIdeas.idea: The check split one person into two: different names mean no merge, the opposite error to the Tallentires, a missing thread instead of a false one
Resolve on evidence beyond the name: a marriage record or alias linking the names, plus the same school, role and dates
Send unclear merges to a person for review, and record each merge decision with its evidence so it can be undone

coldCase.model: The merge check did its job too literally. It joins two mentions only when the name, place and dates agree, and a woman who married in 1922 appears under two names, so the graph split one person into two nodes: the opposite error to the Tallentires, a missing thread instead of a false one. The name alone can't settle either case. I'd let the check use more evidence than the name: a marriage record or an alias table that links her maiden name to her married name, plus the same school, the same role and dates that fit one life. Where the evidence is thin, don't merge automatically: send it for review by a person, and record each merge decision with its evidence so it can be undone if a later record disagrees.
